Deliverable 01

Interview plan

Who I'd talk to before building, why, and the questions I'd most want answered. Each group ends with what its answers would change in the design, because an interview that can't change the build isn't worth scheduling yet.

The order I'd run them

Problem first, then feasibility, then the guardrails before anything touches a real client.

Week 1 · Frame the problem

Execs, CPLs, agency producers

Where deals die, what an agent's time is worth, and why cyber doesn't get raised today.

Week 2 · Test feasibility

Ops / wholesale, carriers, agency-system vendors

What data exists, how indications come back, and which controls carriers treat as gates.

Before a pilot · Guardrails and the end customer

Compliance / legal, business owners

Consent and licensing lines, plus whether owners would actually take the call or answer the link.

What each group covers

Topic coverage across the questions below. A filled dot means a group is the main source on that topic; a ring means it adds a second view.

Groups and questions

UKON executives

Week 1

Why: they set the economics and define what "worked" means. Without that, I'd be optimizing the wrong metric.

  1. Which agencies and client segments matter most this year?
  2. What does a bound cyber policy earn UKON, and what does it earn the agent?
  3. Where do deals die today: before the quote, at the proposal, or at the application?
  4. What does success look like in 12 months, and which number would you check first?

Changes: which clients the renewal queue ranks first, and the target for agent minutes per bound policy.

Cyber Practice Leaders (CPLs)

Week 1

Why: they support agents day to day and own coverage accuracy. They know where agents get stuck and where a wrong answer becomes a liability.

  1. Where does your time go for each policy that binds?
  2. Which objections come up most, and which answers actually work?
  3. Which questions should an agent never answer on their own?
  4. What makes a submission "clean," and what makes one bounce?
  5. Would you review flagged estimates if it saved you time later in the process?

Changes: the approved objection library, the escalation rules, and whether UKON's team (rather than the agent) absorbs the review work.

UKON ops / wholesale

Week 2

Why: they handle submissions to carriers, so they know what data carriers really require and where it breaks.

  1. How do indications come back today: API, portal, or email?
  2. Do carriers accept a revenue band for an indication, or do they need a number?
  3. What causes declines and re-quotes most often?
  4. How long does it take from submission to indication?

Changes: which carrier integrations come first, and how precise the revenue estimate has to be.

Agency producers & account managers

Week 1

Why: they're the primary users. If this adds work for them, it won't get used, whatever else it does.

  1. What's in your agency system for a renewing client: revenue, payroll, headcount, email domain? Would you share an export?
  2. Why don't you bring up cyber today?
  3. How long does a cyber quote take you now, start to finish?
  4. How many clients renew each month, and how many get offered cyber?
  5. Would you run a recorded intake call, or rather send the client a link?

Changes: the order of the revenue sources, whether the call or the link is the default, and the baseline for the success metric.

Business owners

Before a pilot

Why: they decide whether to buy, and they aren't technical. The proposal pack only works if it answers their questions in their order.

  1. What would make you take a cyber conversation seriously?
  2. What do you need to see before you'd buy: the price, examples, what's covered?
  3. Would you rather answer questions on a call or through a link on your phone?
  4. Who handles your IT, and would you want them involved?

Changes: the order of sections in the pack, and the intake channel.

Carriers / underwriters

Week 2

Why: they price and write the policy. Their minimum data and their hard gates decide what intake has to collect.

  1. What's the minimum data you need for an indication?
  2. Which security controls are hard gates: MFA, backups, endpoint detection?
  3. How do you treat answers from a recorded call compared with a signed application?
  4. Can indications be requested and returned by API?

Changes: the intake question bank and how the application gets pre-filled.

Compliance / legal

Before a pilot

Why: recorded calls, AI-written client material and insurance data each carry legal lines that have to be drawn before a real client sees anything.

  1. What are the recording consent rules, state by state, for intake calls?
  2. Where is the licensing line for AI-written material a client reads?
  3. How long can we keep call transcripts, and where must they live?

Changes: the consent script, the approved-language library, and data retention.

Agency-system vendors

Week 2

Why: the renewal queue depends on reading the agency's own records. Whether that's an API, an export or nothing at all decides how Stage 0 works.

  1. What renewal and client data can a partner read, and how: API or export?
  2. How are agency permissions handled, so an agent only sees their own agency's clients?
  3. Does the system show existing cyber coverage, including endorsements on other policies?

Changes: whether the renewal queue can be automatic, and how existing coverage gets filtered out.

Open question 1: what happens after a policy is bound?

The brief stops at "bound". But the business only works if the policy is still in force a year later, and the client's security can drift during the year. What I know going in, and what I'd ask.

What's publicly known

  • Some carriers monitor during the policy year. Coalition, for example, says it scans the internet continuously and sends policyholders personalized alerts with recommended fixes (Coalition). This varies by carrier; many don't.
  • Renewal is re-underwriting, not a rubber stamp. A new application and fresh evidence of controls (MFA, endpoint detection, tested backups, an incident response plan). Missing proof leads to a price jump or a decline (CyberDuo, Dec 2025, citing Aon and carrier applications).
  • The application is a legal representation. If a control the client said was in place wasn't, a claim can be disputed. That's why the prototype never turns a hedged answer into "yes".

What I don't know yet

  • Which of UKON's carriers scan after bind, how often, and who gets the alert: the client, the agent, or UKON?
  • Does anyone check mid-term that the controls from the application are still in place?
  • Who owns the client between bind and renewal: the producer, the account manager, or UKON's CPL?
  • How many cyber policies UKON writes are still in force at year two, and why the others aren't.
AskQuestionWhat the answer changes
CarriersDo you scan or monitor insureds after bind? How often, and who receives the findings? What happens if a control on the application lapses mid-term?Whether the workbench needs a "post-bind alerts" queue, and whether alerts go to the agent too.
CarriersAt renewal, what do you re-check: a new application, a rescan, attestations, evidence?How much of the intake can carry forward a year; what to collect again.
CPLsWhen a claim is disputed, how often is it because the application didn't match reality?How hard to push the "confirm, don't assume" guardrails, and which answers need evidence.
Ops / wholesaleWhat share of cyber policies renew at year two? Of the ones that don't, who ended it: the client or the carrier?Whether retention is a bigger lever than new sales.
Producers / AMsWhat do you do for a cyber client between bind and renewal? Do you hear about carrier alerts?Who the post-bind features are for.
Business ownersIf your insurer told you mid-year that something on your network was exposed, what would you do with that?Whether a security check-in is a reason to stay, or just noise.
Design idea to test: a mid-term check-in six months after bind. Re-run the public checks (email security, exposed services), confirm the application's controls are still true, and give the agent a reason to call that isn't a bill. It turns renewal from re-underwriting into a formality.

Open question 2: why don't small businesses buy cyber, or keep it?

The brief's explanation is distribution: agents don't bring it up because getting a client from "no cyber" to "protected" is too much manual work. I think that's real but incomplete, and I'd test it against the other explanations before betting the roadmap on it.

Two different problems hide in one question. The brief's "renewal window" is the renewal of the client's other policies, the moment to sell cyber for the first time. A client dropping a cyber policy at its own renewal is a retention problem, with different causes.

Carriers say no: the client can't show MFA, endpoint detection or tested backups, so it's declined or re-priced at renewalMissing controls are standard refusal criteria; missing proof means price shock or decline (CyberDuo, Dec 2025). Argo: 42% of SMEs doubted their own security (2017).Ops: of non-renewals, how many were the carrier's decision, and which control was missing?A remediation path before renewal: what to fix, with the IT provider, 60 days out.

The prototype's intake assumes owners need help translating questions.CPLs and ops: where do applications stall, and on which questions?More of the application pre-filled; the IT provider answers the technical part directly.

My current read, with low confidence until we see UKON's own data: first-time adoption is mostly the brief's distribution problem plus price; dropping a policy is mostly price at renewal and carriers re-underwriting controls. The one number that would settle it fastest is ops' split of non-renewals into "client walked" and "carrier declined", with reasons.
